standard.title: Explore language and culture connections
standard.description: explore connections between language and culture
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have no prior formal experience with the target language or its communities. They bring general awareness of their own cultural practices and language from home and community.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students notice connections between the target language and the cultural practices of target language communities, recognising that language reflects who people are and how they live.

nodes.label: Noticing that language reflects cultural practices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice that target language words, greetings and expressions reflect cultural practices — that language is not just a code but carries meaning about how people live and relate.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one target language word or expression that reflects a cultural practice and describe what it tells them about how people in that community do things.
nodes.typical_width: Notice cultural meaning in target language greetings, forms of address, and expressions related to celebrations and food; explore how forms of address signal respect and relationship; engage with authentic resources about target language community practices.
wider: Compare a target language community practice (e.g. a celebration, a greeting convention) with a practice from their own background — identify what is similar and different
Notice how the target language is spoken in many different places and communities — same language, different contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: The foundational insight that language and culture are connected is the conceptual entry point for all language-and-culture work in subsequent bands. Students who treat the target language purely as a code cannot engage with cultural meaning or intercultural comparison in later years.

response_modes.reason: The connection between language and culture is most visible when students encounter multiple examples across different cultural domains — greetings, food, celebrations, address conventions. Single-example exposure produces surface noticing; varied examples build the generalisation that language always carries cultural meaning.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one target language word or expression that connects to a cultural practice and describes the connection
Can explain, with support, why the same thing might be expressed or done differently in target language communities and their own community

nodes.label: Noticing linguistic diversity and First Nations language connections
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice that many languages exist in the world — including languages of First Nations Australians — and that the target language is one language spoken by diverse communities.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that the target language is spoken in many places and that their local area has its own First Nations language(s) — connecting both to the idea that language is tied to people and place.
nodes.typical_width: Use the AIATSIS map to notice First Nations languages in their local area; recognise that local place names and landmarks may originate in First Nations languages; understand that some people speak more than one language; explore target language community diversity.
wider: Research one local First Nations language word for a place name and one target language word for a cultural concept — compare what each reveals about the relationship between language and place or culture
Discuss what it means to speak more than one language — drawing on class members' language backgrounds and comparing with target language community contexts

response_modes.reason: Linguistic diversity awareness develops through encountering diverse language examples — First Nations languages, home languages of class members, target language regional diversity. Multiple examples across different language communities build the concept of linguistic diversity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting target language learning to First Nations language acknowledgement and to students' own linguistic backgrounds positions language learning as part of a broader awareness of diversity and place. This connection — made at Foundation — establishes a values orientation toward multilingualism that enriches the whole sequence.
success_criteria: Identifies that the target language is spoken by people in many different places
Identifies that First Nations Australians have their own languages connected to Country and can locate at least one example relevant to their local area
